narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 80.3% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—roughly four chances in five. For an admissions decision, that high failure risk outweighed the rest of your profile.

The most influential factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That relatively low standing pushed the prediction strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year class standing was the next most important factor: you were in the first decile, again well below the average for accepted students, and it also pushed toward failure. Your family income bracket was the third most important factor; coming from a high-income family nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, but not enough to overcome the two class-standing signals. Your LSAT score was close to the accepted-student average and your undergraduate GPA was above it, but these did not outweigh the strongest factors.

To move forward, ask admissions whether an appeal or individualized review is available and provide any context that may explain your early academic standing. Meet with an academic advisor to build a concrete improvement plan, consider delaying reapplication until you have stronger recent academic evidence, and use structured bar-prep diagnostics to address likely exam risks.
